passage:
Looking back at second year, I can see exactly what I was doing. My marks in two papers dropped, and the hostel fee reminder came three times. Each time I thought, "It'll sort itself out. Something will turn up." When the student counsellor emailed, I archived it without opening it. Not looking felt strangely calm.
My roommate Divyansh asked once whether I'd paid the fee. I changed the subject to the cricket match.
Then the notice went up: fees unpaid by Friday meant no hall ticket. My stomach dropped. On Thursday I finally opened that email, sat in the counsellor's office, and learnt about an instalment option I could have known about weeks earlier.
— Binita

qa.q: What did Binita do with the counsellor's email?
qa.a: Archived it without opening it.

qa.q: Why did not looking feel strangely calm to Binita?
qa.a: Avoiding the email and reminders kept the dread at a distance, so it felt calmer than facing falling marks and an unpaid fee.

qa.q: What could Binita have done at the first fee reminder instead?
qa.a: Opening the counsellor's email or asking the office straight away could have turned up the instalment option weeks earlier, with far less panic.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have sensed when Binita changed the subject?
qa.a: Divyansh may have sensed something was wrong with the fee and felt unsure whether to push or let it go.

grounding: A student looks back on dodging falling marks, fee reminders and the counsellor's email until a hall-ticket deadline forced action.

passage:
Student support note: Pallavi, B.Com second year
I emailed Pallavi on 3 and 17 September after her attendance and internal marks dropped. No reply. A friend of hers told me Pallavi kept saying, "It'll sort itself out, I'm just tired."
On 1 October the accounts office flagged unpaid fees; exam registration closes on the 10th. Today, the 8th, Pallavi came in holding the office printout. She said she had seen my emails in her inbox and couldn't make herself click them.
I didn't lecture. We made three calls together: the accounts office, her class mentor, and her father. By the end she was breathing more easily.
Next: weekly check-in on Mondays.
— Himani

qa.q: When did the accounts office flag Pallavi's unpaid fees?
qa.a: On 1 October.

qa.q: Why couldn't Pallavi make herself click the emails?
qa.a: Opening them would have made the falling marks and fees real, and not looking kept the dread down until the deadline came close.

qa.q: What choice by Himani helped once Pallavi came in?
qa.a: Himani skipped the lecture and made the three calls alongside her, turning a frightening pile into a few concrete steps.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's friend have felt hearing 'It'll sort itself out'?
qa.a: The friend may have been worried but unsure what to do, sensing that things weren't really fine.

grounding: A support officer's note records a student ignoring falling marks, unpaid fees and emails until the registration deadline brought her in.

passage:
12 March, 11 pm
Didn't open the portal again today. I know the mid-sem marks are up. I know they're low; Sarika checked hers and went quiet when she looked at me. Fee reminder number four is sitting unread too.
Told myself: next week things will calm down and I'll deal with it then. Somehow that thought makes my shoulders drop, even though nothing has changed.
And the counsellor's email. Subject line: "Checking in." Skipped it. Watched three episodes of a baking show instead.
Sarika just told me the fee window closes Friday. Friday. That's three days away.
Okay. Tomorrow I open the portal. Maybe the email too.
— Lavanya

qa.q: What was the subject line of the counsellor's email?
qa.a: "Checking in."

qa.q: Why does the thought 'next week things will calm down' make Lavanya's shoulders drop?
qa.a: Putting it off to next week brings instant relief from the dread, even though the marks and fees haven't changed at all.

qa.q: What would be a workable first step for Lavanya tomorrow?
qa.a: Opening the portal and sending the counsellor a one-line reply, so someone can help before Friday.

qa.q: What might Sarika feel when she tells Lavanya the fee window closes Friday?
qa.a: Sarika is probably worried for Lavanya and may have been waiting for the right moment to say it.

grounding: A student's diary shows unopened marks, fee reminders and a skipped counsellor email until a Friday deadline starts to force the issue.

qa.q: When did the fee portal close?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth keep saying it would sort itself out?
qa.a: Not looking at the email and the fees helped him avoid dread, even though the problems were growing.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Siddharth choose after it?
qa.a: The closed portal and blocked hall ticket forced him to look; he then agreed to go to the office with Pradeep and book the counsellor.

qa.q: What was it like for Pradeep to watch Siddharth avoid the problem?
qa.a: Pradeep seemed worried but unsure how to push, sending reminders and then offering to go with him once the deadline hit.

grounding: A chat shows a student ignoring falling marks, fees and the counsellor's email until a deadline forces the issue.

passage: In the girls' hostel of the small college in Hassan, Indu, nineteen, had tucked the counsellor's letter inside her economics book, unopened. Her internal marks had slid from sixties to thirties. The hostel fee slip was two months old. "It'll sort itself out," she told her roommate Payal, and went to the temple fair with the juniors every evening that week, laughing a little too loudly. Payal noticed she'd stopped studying at night and slept badly. On Monday morning a notice went up outside the office: students with unpaid fees would not get exam hall tickets after Wednesday. Indu's name was on it. She stood staring for a long time. Then she went back to the room, opened the economics book, and read the counsellor's letter for the first time. "Payal," she said quietly, "will you come with me?"

qa.q: Where had Indu tucked the counsellor's letter?
qa.a: Inside her economics book, unopened.

qa.q: Why did Indu go to the temple fair every evening and laugh a little too loudly?
qa.a: Keeping busy and cheerful helped her push away the dread about her marks and fees, so she didn't have to look at them.

qa.q: What forced Indu to act, and what could have helped earlier?
qa.a: The notice with her name forced her; reading the counsellor's letter when it came, or telling Payal sooner, could have helped before it became urgent.

qa.q: How might Payal have seen Indu during that week?
qa.a: Payal noticed the stopped studying and poor sleep, and was probably worried but unsure how to help until Indu asked.

grounding: A student ignores falling marks, unpaid fees and a counsellor's letter until a deadline forces her to face them.
